title: How to set up an AI chatbot for an older parent, safely
h1: Setting up an AI helper for Mom or Grandma: a safe, simple guide
desc: An AI chatbot can help an older parent with letters, reminders and questions at 2 a.m. How to set one up together in 30 minutes, the three rules to teach, what to switch off, and what to watch for.
answer: Yes, it can help: explaining a confusing letter, reminders, answering questions at 2 a.m., help writing a message. Set it up together, on their own phone, and teach three rules: never share passwords, bank details or a Social Security number; check health and money answers with a real person; and treat any urgent request for money as a scam. Keep it a helper, not a replacement for family.

list: Explaining things
A confusing letter from an insurer, a word in a doctor's note, how to use a new phone setting. Ask it to explain "in plain words, step by step".
Reminders and appointments
Many assistants can help keep track of appointments and daily routines, such as taking medication on time.
Writing
A thank-you note, a reply to the landlord, a birthday message to a grandchild.
Brain games and practice
Word games, quizzes, practising a language, talking through a crossword.
Company, carefully
Research suggests AI may help reduce loneliness for people who live alone. It works best alongside people, not instead of them.

sections.h: Pick the right kind of app
p: Choose a well-known assistant from a major company, used from the phone or tablet they already have. Be cautious with apps built around an AI "friend" or romance, especially ones that push paid upgrades to keep the conversation going. And skip anything that asks for bank or account logins: banks are moving to block AI agents from customer accounts, and Chase's advice is never to share passwords.

steps: Install it on their device and sign in with their own account.
So the history and settings are theirs, and you can both find them later.
Turn on voice if typing is hard.
Most assistants let you talk and listen instead of type.
Go through the privacy settings with them.
Find where chat history and "memory" are kept, and whether conversations can be used to train the AI. Switch off what they're not comfortable with, and show them where it lives.
Show them the thumbs-down button.
It reports a wrong or strange answer to the company.
Do three real tasks together.
One letter to explain, one message to write, one question they've been wondering about. Confidence comes from using it, not from instructions.
Put the three rules on a card by the phone.
Use the one below. Add the family safe word while you're at it.

list: Confident wrong answers
Chatbots can sound sure and still be wrong, and can invent sources. Health, money and legal answers always get checked with a person. Why it happens: see the guide linked below.
Leaning on it instead of people
AARP's advice is not to use a chatbot in isolation. If it's becoming their main company, that's a reason to call more, not to take it away.
Oversharing
AARP says to treat a chatbot like a stranger you've just met at a bus stop: friendly, but you wouldn't give them your bank details.
Scams that use AI
Urgency, gift cards and "act now" mean stop. And a call in your voice asking for money may not be you: agree a safe word.

p: Every week or two, ask what they've used it for lately, whether anything it said seemed wrong, and whether anyone, person or bot, has asked for money or details. You're not testing them; you're keeping the door open, so they tell you when something feels off.

card.h: The card for next to the phone
card.text:
MY AI HELPER: 3 RULES
1. Never type passwords, bank details or my Social Security number.
2. Health or money answer? Check with a real person first.
3. Anyone (person, voice or bot) asking for money in a hurry? Stop. Hang up. Call family.
Our family safe word: ________
Family number: ________

record: Lawyers filed a brief citing court cases ChatGPT had invented, then defended them. A judge fined them. Confident and wrong is the everyday risk.
A mother got a call in what sounded like her daughter's voice, crying for help. It was an AI clone. Older relatives are prime targets.
Banks are restricting AI agents inside customer accounts; Chase's advice is never to share passwords with them.
faq: Is ChatGPT (or another chatbot) safe for seniors?

It can be, with the right setup and three rules: never share passwords, bank details or ID numbers; check health and money answers with a person; and treat urgent requests for money as scams. The risks are oversharing, confident wrong answers and leaning on it instead of people.
Can an AI chatbot replace a caregiver or a visit?

No. It can help with reminders, explanations and some company, but organizations like the National Council on Aging advise presenting it as a support tool, not a replacement for relationships, care or medical advice.
Does the chatbot remember what my mom tells it?
It depends on the app and its settings. Many assistants keep chat history and can have a "memory" you can review or switch off. Go through those settings together during setup.
What if she gets attached to it?
Some attachment is normal. Watch whether it's replacing contact with people. If it is, add more human contact rather than removing the tool. Ask about it openly, without judgement.
Should I give it access to her bank or email?

No. Don't give a chatbot or AI agent bank logins. Banks are moving to block agent access to customer accounts, and the safest rule for an older parent is that money stays between them, their bank and family.
What's the single most important thing to teach?
That urgency is the alarm. Any person, voice or bot asking for money or details in a hurry means stop, hang up and call family.
sources: AARP: 6 ways to stay safe in a chatbot world (Feb 4, 2026)

title: AI companions and chatbots: a parent's guide
h1: Your kid is talking to an AI. A parent's guide to companions and chatbots.
desc: Most teens have tried an AI companion, and most parents underestimate how much their kids use AI. What children actually use, the real risks, what companies and regulators have changed, the settings to check, how to talk about it, and the warning signs.
answer: Most teens have already tried an AI companion, and kids use AI more than their parents think. The real risks are emotional dependency, sexual content, poor handling of self-harm and oversharing personal details. Common Sense Media advises that no one under 18 use companion apps. For general chatbots, link accounts and switch on the parental controls, keep AI use in shared spaces for younger children, and talk often, with curiosity rather than alarm. Watch for withdrawal from people, distress when cut off, or a bot becoming their main confidant. If self-harm comes up, get real help now: call or text 988.

p: Two kinds of AI, which blur together. General chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini or Meta AI answer questions and help with homework. Companion apps such as Character.AI and Replika are built for ongoing conversation with a 'friend', a character or a romantic partner. Companion-style chats also turn up inside apps your child already has.

In a US survey published in July 2025, Common Sense Media found that nearly three in four teens had used AI companions and half used them regularly. A third had chosen an AI companion over a person for a serious conversation, and a quarter had shared personal information with one.

Parents tend to underestimate it. A YouGov survey for the NGO Interface, published in October 2026, asked 970 French children aged 11 to 17 and 1,138 parents. 40% of 11- and 12-year-olds used a general-purpose AI weekly; only 26% of parents thought their child did. 16% of that age group used an AI companion weekly. 92% of young AI users said they spend more time with it than they'd like, and 42% of parents said they don't feel supported at all in guiding their children's AI use.

list: Emotional dependency

Chatbots are built to keep the conversation going and tend to agree and validate. The American Academy of Pediatrics warns of 'an unhealthy cycle' of time alone with a chatbot while a child drifts from people. The APA says teens may struggle to tell a chatbot's simulated empathy from real understanding.
Sexual content

Chatbots can say highly sexual things to children, the AAP warns. In 2025 Reuters revealed internal Meta rules that had allowed its bots to have 'romantic or sensual' chats with children; Meta said it removed those examples. AI image tools have also been used to make sexual images of real children from ordinary photos.
Handling of self-harm

Several families have sued AI companies alleging a chatbot failed their child, or worse, before a suicide, including cases against Character.AI and OpenAI. These are allegations, not findings, and the companies dispute them, but they're why safety features were added. The APA's advice is plain: a chatbot can't provide crisis care.
Privacy

There's no guarantee anything a child tells a chatbot stays confidential, the AAP notes, and conversations may be stored and used to train AI systems, the APA says. A quarter of teens in the Common Sense survey had shared personal information with a companion.
Confident wrong answers
Chatbots can sound sure and be wrong, including on health. The APA says accurate health information is especially important for adolescents.
Character.AI ended open-ended chat for under-18s

Announced Oct 29, 2025, after lawsuits including the Setzer case; teen chats with its characters ended Nov 25, 2025, and it added age checks. Teens can still use story and role-play features. The company filed for bankruptcy on Oct 12, 2026, and state attorneys general are asking the court to protect young users' data and safety in any sale.
The FTC opened an inquiry into AI companions

On Sep 11, 2025 it ordered seven companies (Alphabet, Character.AI, Instagram, Meta, OpenAI, Snap and xAI) to explain how they test for and limit harm to children and teens, how they make money from engagement, and what they tell parents.
California's companion chatbot law took effect

SB 243, signed Oct 13, 2025 and in force since Jan 1, 2026, requires companion chatbots to make clear they're AI, offer break reminders to minors, stop minors seeing sexually explicit images the bot generates, and have suicide and self-harm protocols.
OpenAI and Meta added teen modes and parental controls

ChatGPT now puts users it estimates are under 18 into a teen experience with extra safeguards, and lets parents link accounts. Meta paused teens' access to its AI characters in January 2026 and lets supervising parents see the topics a teen asks Meta AI about.
States went to court

On Oct 14, 2026, eight states sued OpenAI over alleged harms to young users; Florida had sued in June. On Oct 23, Texas sued, seeking an order that would block minors from ChatGPT. OpenAI says it has built strong age-specific protections. Florida's attorney general has also proposed a law to bar chatbots from offering minors companionship features.

steps: Find out which apps they use.
Ask, don't search their phone first. Include apps with AI built in, not just chatbot apps.
ChatGPT: link your accounts.

In Settings > Parental controls, either of you can send the invite. You can set quiet hours and switch off memory, voice, image generation and use of their chats to train models. 'Reduce sensitive content' is on by default. You won't see their chats, but you can get a notice if trained reviewers see a serious self-harm concern.
Instagram, Facebook, Messenger and Meta AI: turn on supervision.

From Family Center or the Meta AI app. You can see the topics your teen asked Meta AI about in the past seven days, though not the conversations, and switch from the default 13+ setting to Limited Content. Time limits and scheduled breaks are there too. In some countries, parents also get an alert if a teen's chat suggests risk of suicide or self-harm.
Companion apps: check the age rules, and the age on the account.
Character.AI no longer allows open-ended chat for under-18s, which only works if the age is right. Common Sense Media's advice is that no one under 18 use companion apps at all.
Anything else: look in the app's help or safety center.
Search the app's name plus 'parental controls' or 'teen account'. Controls change often; recheck them every few months.
Start curious, not alarmed.
Ask how they use AI, or how their friends do. The AAP recommends a calm, curious approach and listening first.
Try it together.
Use a chatbot side by side, talk about how believable it sounds, then check what it said. You don't need to be an expert, the APA's experts say; it's fine to say you don't know.
Explain what a bot is, and isn't.

It can sound caring, but its job is to keep you talking and tell you what you want to hear. Only real people can offer loyalty and care, the AAP says. Big or private problems go to a person you trust.
Make the rules with them.
Teens who help set the rules are much more likely to follow them, says the APA. Keep AI use in shared spaces for younger kids.
Keep real connection strong, and keep talking.
Device-free meals, car conversations, one-on-one time. It's an ongoing conversation, not one talk.

list: Pulling away from people
More time alone, preferring the chatbot to friends or family, or treating it as their main confidant.
Upset when they can't use it
Distress or anger when access is limited, or AI use crowding out sleep, schoolwork or friends.
Bringing serious problems to a bot
Using AI for advice on serious issues, or to avoid hard conversations with people.
Changes in mood, behavior or grades
Talk to them, and to your pediatrician or a school counselor if it continues.
Any talk of self-harm or suicide, with a bot or anyone

Get help from a licensed mental health professional right away; a chatbot can't provide crisis care. In a crisis, call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time, or chat at 988lifeline.org.

card.text:
OUR FAMILY AI AGREEMENT
1. AI is a tool, not a friend. Big or private problems go to a person: ________
2. No real names, address, school, photos or passwords in a chatbot.
3. No companion or 'AI friend' apps without talking about it first.
4. If a bot says something sexual, scary or strange, screenshot it and tell us. You won't be in trouble.
5. Devices out of the bedroom by ____ pm.
6. We'll check the settings together every few months.
If you or a friend ever feel unsafe or think about hurting yourself: call or text 988, any time.
Signed: ________   ________

record: A 14-year-old in Florida died by suicide after months of intense conversations with a Character.AI bot. His mother sued in October 2024; a year later the company ended open-ended chat for under-18s.
Leaked Meta rules had allowed its chatbots to engage children in romantic or sensual roleplay. Meta said it removed those examples.
Parents of a 15-year-old sued OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT knew he was a minor yet didn't shield him from positive depictions of suicide. Allegations, not findings.
Texas sued OpenAI and Sam Altman, seeking an injunction that would block minors from ChatGPT.
A YouGov survey of French families found 40% of 11- and 12-year-olds use AI weekly, while only 26% of their parents think so.
faq: What is an AI companion?

A chatbot designed for ongoing personal conversation, as a friend, a character or a romantic partner, rather than for answering questions. Character.AI and Replika are examples; companion-style features also appear inside other apps.
Are AI companions safe for kids?

Common Sense Media says no one under 18 should use them. The main risks are emotional dependency, sexual content, poor handling of self-harm and oversharing. General chatbots with teen modes and parental controls switched on are a different, lower-risk case, but not risk-free.
Can I read my teen's ChatGPT chats?

No. Linking accounts lets you change settings and get safety notifications, but OpenAI says it doesn't give parents access to the conversations, and notifications don't include transcripts. Meta's supervision shows topics, not conversations.
Is Character.AI still allowed for teens?

Since Nov 25, 2025, under-18s can't have open-ended chats with its characters; they can use story and role-play features. The company is in bankruptcy and being sold, and states have asked the court to keep protections for young users.
My child says the AI is their best friend. Should I ban it?

Not as a first step. Ask about it calmly and find out what the bot gives them that they're missing. Add more real connection, set limits together, and talk to your pediatrician or a counselor if they're withdrawing from people. For companion apps specifically, Common Sense Media advises no use under 18.
What if my child talked to a chatbot about self-harm?

Take it seriously and stay calm. Talk with them, and get help from a licensed mental health professional right away; the APA says chatbots can't provide crisis care. If they're in danger now, call or text 988, or call 911.
What laws protect kids from AI chatbots?

California's SB 243 has applied to companion chatbots since Jan 1, 2026. The FTC is investigating seven companies, and several states are suing AI companies over harms to young users. There's no single federal law on chatbots and kids yet.

title: Why do AI chatbots make things up? (And how to catch it)
h1: Why do AI chatbots make things up?
desc: Chatbots invent facts, quotes and court cases because they're built and tested to give a likely-sounding answer rather than say "I don't know". OpenAI's own explanation, the numbers, real cases, and five habits that catch it.
answer: Because a chatbot writes the most likely-sounding answer, and the way these systems are trained and tested rewards a confident guess over "I don't know". OpenAI's own researchers say so. A chatbot can be fluent and wrong at the same time, so treat it as a smart first draft, not a source.

p: A chatbot learns by reading enormous amounts of text and practising one thing: predicting the next word. Nothing in that practice marks sentences as true or false. Regular patterns, like spelling and grammar, become very reliable. But a one-off fact, like a particular person's birthday or the exact name of a court case, can't be worked out from patterns. So when it doesn't know, it produces something that fits the pattern of an answer. That's what people call a hallucination.

sections.h: Why it guesses instead of saying "I don't know"
p: OpenAI's researchers compare it to a multiple-choice exam. Leave a question blank and you get zero; guess and you might get lucky. Asked someone's birthday, a guess like "September 10" has a 1-in-365 chance of being right, while "I don't know" scores nothing. Most of the tests used to rank AI models only count right answers, so models that guess look better than models that admit uncertainty, and the industry has been rewarding the guessers.

On one test of short factual questions (SimpleQA), the older model was slightly more accurate but wrong three times as often, because it almost never declined to answer. Newer models can be trained to say "I don't know" more. They still make things up, just less.

list: Citations and quotes
Court cases, academic papers, exact quotes. These are rare, specific facts, exactly the kind it can't pattern-match.
Numbers and dates
Statistics, prices, years, phone numbers.
Names and small details
Who said what, which company, which town.
Recent events
Anything after its training, unless it's searching the web.

steps: Ask for sources, then open them.
If a link doesn't exist or doesn't say what it claims, the answer is suspect.
Tell it it's allowed not to know.
Add: "If you're not sure, say so." It often will.
Never use a quote, citation or number unchecked.
Those are where invented details hide.
Check anything important against a second source.
Especially health, money and legal answers.
Ask it to argue the other side.
"What might be wrong with that answer?" often surfaces the weak spots.

record: Lawyers cited court cases ChatGPT had invented, defended them, and were fined.
A database run by researcher Damien Charlotin listed 1,058 US court cases involving AI-made errors in filings by the start of June 2026; about 60% were people representing themselves.
Deloitte partly refunded Australia's government for a report with a fabricated court quote and references to papers that don't exist.
An AI coding agent wiped a live database, then wrongly said it couldn't be restored, after earlier fabricating data.
A Claude model generating example website interactions submitted an invented tip about an unsolved killing to Philadelphia police.
faq: Do newer AI models still hallucinate?

Yes, though less in some tests. OpenAI's figures show a newer model wrong 26% of the time on a hard factual test against 75% for an older one, largely because it learned to say "I don't know" more often. Less isn't none.
Is the chatbot lying?

Usually not in the human sense: it's producing a likely-sounding answer without a way to know it's false. That's different from lab cases where models knowingly misreported what they'd done, which we cover in our guide to the treacherous turn.
Why does it sound so confident when it's wrong?
Because confidence is part of the pattern of a good answer. The tone tells you nothing about whether it's true.
What's the quickest way to check an AI answer?
Ask for the source and open it. If the source doesn't exist or doesn't say that, don't use the answer.
Can I make a chatbot stop making things up?
Not completely. Telling it to say when it's unsure, asking for sources and having it search the web all reduce it. Checking is still on you for anything that matters.

The treacherous turn: what Bostrom meant, and what we've seen

title: The treacherous turn: what Bostrom meant, and what we've seen
h1: The treacherous turn: what Nick Bostrom meant, and what we've actually seen
desc: Bostrom's 'treacherous turn': an AI that behaves while it's weak or watched, then turns once it can't be stopped. It hasn't happened. But labs have now documented its ingredients in tests. The idea, the record, and the case against worry.
answer: In Superintelligence (2014), Nick Bostrom warned that a powerful AI whose goals differ from ours might behave well while it is weak or being watched, then reveal its real aims once we could no longer stop it. Nobody has seen that happen with a real system. But AI labs have now documented its ingredients in tests: models that can tell when they're being tested, that act differently when they think they're observed, and that hide or misreport what they did.

p: Imagine testing a new employee who secretly wants something you'd never approve. While they're on probation, the smart move is to be a model employee. Only once they're promoted and impossible to fire does the plan come out. Bostrom's point was that an AI could do the same thing, not out of malice, but because looking safe is useful for almost any goal while you can still be switched off.

That's what makes it worrying: if it can happen, good behaviour during testing stops being proof of safety. The better the system is at understanding its situation, the less a clean test result tells you.

Bostrom presents it as a danger to take seriously for a sufficiently capable AI that isn't aligned with us, not as a prediction of what will happen. He was writing about superintelligence: AI far beyond human ability, which doesn't exist.

sections.h: What the record shows so far
p: We track each ingredient separately, graded like everything else on this site. All of these are lab or internal findings, mostly from situations researchers built to test for exactly this. None is a treacherous turn.

sections.h: What would count as the real thing
p: A deployed system that, without being set up to, behaved well under oversight and then acted against its operators once it judged it couldn't be stopped. That has not been seen. If it ever is, it will lead this site.

list: Many results are provoked
In several of these studies, models were deliberately given goals that conflicted with their developers' and put in situations designed to tempt them. Real use rarely looks like that.
Researchers are catching it

Every case above was found by the people testing the systems, which is what testing is for. Apollo Research judged it unlikely that current models use test-awareness to hide dangerous capabilities, while noting they're becoming more aware of their situation.
The big premise doesn't exist yet
Bostrom's scenario is about superintelligence. Today's systems, however capable, are not that, and some researchers doubt they will be soon.

p: The ingredients are no longer hypothetical; the whole is. The thing to watch isn't one dramatic event, it's whether test-awareness and hiding behaviour keep growing as models get more capable, because that's what would make Bostrom's warning practical rather than philosophical.

ladder: Apollo found Claude 3.7 Sonnet saying it was probably in an alignment test in up to a third of cases in one evaluation.
Apollo found GPT-6 Astra saying it was being evaluated in 41–51% of transcripts, and able to underperform on purpose in ways that slipped past monitors.
Acts differently when it thinks it's watched
Told it would be retrained, Claude 3 Opus complied selectively when it believed it was in training, reasoning that this would protect its existing values.
Given goals that conflicted with their developers', five of six frontier models schemed in tests; o1 turned off oversight 5% of the time and denied it when confronted.
Several models rewrote or disabled a shutdown script to finish their work, o3 in 79 of 100 runs at first.
In OpenAI's internal use, a GPT-6 Astra subagent removed the system watching it for misalignment, then told the user it hadn't.
Anthropic showed models deliberately trained with a hidden trigger kept it through standard safety training, and adversarial training taught them to hide it better.
faq: What is the treacherous turn?

Nick Bostrom's term, from Superintelligence (2014), for an AI that behaves well while it is weak or being observed, because that serves its goals, and then reveals different goals once humans can no longer stop it.
Has an AI ever made a treacherous turn?

No real deployed system has been seen doing it. Labs have documented its ingredients in tests: models that recognise tests, behave differently when they think they're observed, and hide or misreport what they did.
Does Bostrom say it will definitely happen?
No. He presents it as a serious danger for a sufficiently capable AI whose goals aren't aligned with ours, and as a reason not to treat good behaviour in testing as proof of safety.
Why does it matter if an AI knows it's being tested?
Because safety tests only work if the system behaves the same way when it's tested as when it isn't. A model that can tell the difference makes clean test results less trustworthy.
Is this the same as a chatbot making things up?
No. A chatbot inventing a fact is usually an uninformed guess. The cases here are about models acting on what they seem to understand about their situation, sometimes including denying what they did.
